passages.happening:
Paul takes up their last question. “Now about the collection for the saints, you are to do as I directed the churches of Galatia” (verse 1).

“On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income, saving it up, so that when I come no collections will be needed” (verse 2).

When he arrives, he will send the people they choose, with letters, to carry their gift to Jerusalem (verse 3). If it seems right, he will go with them (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
‘The saints’ are the believers in Jerusalem, many of them poor. Paul had agreed with the leaders there that he would help: “They only asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do” (Galatians 2:10). He gathered this gift from the mostly Gentile churches of Galatia, Macedonia and Achaia. In Romans he says, “Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to make a contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem” (Romans 15:26).

So this was more than charity. It was Gentile believers caring for Jewish believers they had never met. It showed that the church was one family across the deepest divide of the time.

Paul's plan was simple. Give regularly: ‘on the first day of every week’. Give each one: ‘each of you’. Give in proportion: ‘a portion of his income’, as each had prospered. Save it up, so that nothing would need to be squeezed out of them at the last minute.

‘The first day of every week’ is Sunday, the day Jesus rose. This verse and “On the first day of the week we came together to break bread” (Acts 20:7) are among the earliest signs of believers gathering on that day. The notes on Acts 20 say more.

Paul also guards the money. The church chooses its own people to carry it, with letters. No one could say Paul had taken it for himself.
passages.ot:
The Law taught Israel to care for the poor among them. “For there will never cease to be poor in the land; that is why I am commanding you to open wide your hand to your brother and to the poor and needy in your land” (Deuteronomy 15:11). Proverbs says, “Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender” (Proverbs 19:17).

Giving in proportion was the pattern of Israel's feasts. At the Feast of Weeks, the Old Testament name for Pentecost, Israel gave “a freewill offering that you give in proportion to how the LORD your God has blessed you” (Deuteronomy 16:10). “Everyone must appear with a gift as he is able” (Deuteronomy 16:17).
passages.hard:
Does this passage set a rule for how much Christians should give, such as a tithe, a tenth?

No rule of amount is given here. Paul asks for giving that is regular, planned and in proportion to what each one has. In his next letter he says, “the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what he does not have” (2 Corinthians 8:12), and, “Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

Christians differ on whether a tenth is still the pattern for God's people. The site's notes on Genesis 14, where Abram gives a tenth, set out both views and do not settle it. Both sides agree that what we have comes from God, and that giving should be generous and glad, never forced.
passages.asks: Paul asked for giving that was planned, regular and in proportion. Ask whether your giving is planned or only left to the moment. And ask who are the ‘saints in Jerusalem’ for you: believers far away, unlike you, who are in need.

passages.happening:
Paul will come to Corinth after going through Macedonia (verse 5). Perhaps he will stay, even for the winter, so they can help him on his way (verse 6). He does not want to see them only in passing; he hopes to spend time with them, “if the Lord permits” (verse 7).

“But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, because a great door for effective work has opened to me, even though many oppose me” (verses 8-9).

If Timothy comes, the church must make sure he has nothing to fear, “for he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am” (verse 10). No one should look down on him; they should send him back in peace (verse 11).

“Now about our brother Apollos: I strongly urged him to go to you with the brothers. He was not at all inclined to go now, but he will go when he has the opportunity” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Paul was writing from Ephesus, the great city of the province of Asia. Acts says he worked there for more than two years (Acts 19:10). Pentecost was the feast fifty days after Passover, in early summer.

‘A great door’ and ‘many oppose me’ go together. Acts tells of the opening in Ephesus and also of a riot against Paul there (Acts 19:23-41). Open doors and opposition often came together in Paul's life.

Timothy was Paul's ‘beloved and faithful child in the Lord’ (4:17). Acts says Paul sent him ahead into Macedonia (Acts 19:22). Paul seems to fear that the proud in Corinth would look down on him. So he tells them plainly: he is doing the same work as I am.

Apollos is the teacher some in Corinth had set up as a rival to Paul (1:12). But Paul calls him ‘our brother’, and urged him to visit. There was no rivalry between them. Apollos chose to wait. Paul respects his choice.

‘If the Lord permits’ is the way Paul holds his plans. In fact the plans did change, and 2 Corinthians tells how (2 Corinthians 1:15-16).
passages.ot:
Pentecost was the Old Testament's Feast of Weeks, counted from Passover: “You shall count off fifty days until the day after the seventh Sabbath, and then present an offering of new grain to the LORD” (Leviticus 23:16).

Proverbs teaches the humility of ‘if the Lord permits’: “Many plans are in a man’s heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail” (Proverbs 19:21).
passages.asks: Paul made plans and held them loosely: ‘if the Lord permits’. Ask how you hold your own plans. And notice how Paul speaks of Apollos, whom others set up as his rival: ‘our brother’. Ask who you have been tempted to treat as a rival, and how you could speak of them as Paul does.

passages.happening:
“Be on the alert. Stand firm in the faith. Be men of courage. Be strong” (verse 13). “Do everything in love” (verse 14).

Stephanas and his household were the first converts in Achaia, and they have given themselves to serving the saints (verse 15). Paul urges the church to submit to such people, and to every fellow worker and labourer (verse 16).

Paul is glad that Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus have come, for they have made up for what was lacking from the church (verse 17). “For they refreshed my spirit and yours as well. Show your appreciation, therefore, to such men” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Verses 13 and 14 sound like a soldier's orders. Watch. Stand firm. Be brave. Be strong. Then the last order changes everything: do it all in love. Courage without love is harshness. Love without courage gives way. Paul wants both.

‘Do everything in love’ sums up the letter. The quarrels over leaders, the lawsuits, the meat offered to idols, the Supper, the gifts: in every one, love was the missing thing. Chapter 13 said so at length. Here it is in four words.

Stephanas's household was the first in the province to believe, and Paul baptized them himself (1:16). ‘Achaia’ was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital.

Notice what makes Stephanas a leader. Not wealth, not speaking skill, not spiritual gifts that showed. Service. They ‘devoted themselves to the service of the saints’. Those are the people Paul tells the church to follow.

Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus may have brought the Corinthians' letter to Paul (7:1), and carried this one back; Paul does not say.
passages.ot:
‘Be strong’ echoes God's words to Israel's leaders. Moses told the people, “Be strong and courageous; do not be afraid or terrified of them, for it is the LORD your God who goes with you” (Deuteronomy 31:6). God said to Joshua, “Have I not commanded you to be strong and courageous?” (Joshua 1:9). A psalm joins strength and waiting on God: “Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous” (Psalm 27:14).

The Old Testament, too, joined strength and love. The command to “love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18) stands at the heart of the Law.
passages.asks: Paul joins courage and love: stand firm, and do everything in love. Ask which one you lean toward, and which one you lack. Then think of a Stephanas in your church, someone who serves without being noticed, and find a way this week to ‘show your appreciation’.

passages.happening:
“The churches in the province of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca greet you warmly in the Lord, and so does the church that meets at their house” (verse 19). All the brothers send greetings. “Greet one another with a holy kiss” (verse 20).

Paul takes the pen himself: “This greeting is in my own hand” (verse 21).

“If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse. Come, O Lord!” (verse 22).

“The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen” (verses 23-24).
passages.hearers:
Aquila and Prisca, also called Priscilla, had been with Paul in Corinth when the church began. They were Jews who had come from Italy “because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome” (Acts 18:2). Now they were in Ephesus, with a church meeting in their home. The Corinthians knew them well.

The holy kiss was a greeting among family and close friends. Christians used it as a sign that they were one family. Peter calls it “a kiss of love” (1 Peter 5:14).

Letters were usually written down by a scribe as the author spoke. Paul adds the last lines in his own hand, to show the letter is truly his.

Then verse 22. It holds a curse and a prayer side by side, and the book page lists it among the letter's hard passages. ‘Under a curse’ is anathema, the word for someone handed over to God's judgment. Paul uses it the same way in Galatians: “let him be under a curse” (Galatians 1:8).

‘Come, O Lord’ is not Greek. It is Aramaic, the language Jesus and the first believers in Jerusalem spoke: marana tha. Paul writes it in a Greek letter to a Greek-speaking church without explaining it. They must already have known it, as a prayer they used. The Aramaic can be divided two ways: marana tha, ‘Our Lord, come’, or maran atha, ‘Our Lord has come’. Most read it as a prayer, ‘Our Lord, come’, as the BSB does. The same words appear in an early Christian handbook called the Didache.

That small phrase is a window into the earliest church. ‘Lord’ here, mar in Aramaic, is addressed to Jesus. So the first Aramaic-speaking believers, Jews who prayed to the one God, were already praying to Jesus as Lord and asking him to come. This is a very early witness to how Jesus was worshipped.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament knew things ‘devoted’ or handed over to God, set apart for his judgment. Of Jericho, “The Israelites, however, acted unfaithfully regarding the things devoted to destruction” (Joshua 7:1). The Law warned against bringing a detestable idol home, or “you, like it, will be set apart for destruction” (Deuteronomy 7:26). Paul's anathema stands in that line: it hands a person over to God, not to people.

The closing grace recalls Israel's blessing: “May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you” (Numbers 6:24-25).
passages.hard:
How can a letter about love end with a curse?

‘Let him be under a curse’ is a solemn handing over of a person to God's judgment, not a curse spoken in anger, and not a licence for anyone to curse others. Paul does not tell the church to harm anyone. He leaves judgment to God. It is said of someone who does not love the Lord, at the end of a letter where the church has been asked again and again to love. And in the very next breath he prays, ‘Come, O Lord’, and blesses them with grace and love.

Some readers think verse 22 echoes words the church used when it gathered for worship. No one can be sure. Either way, the curse and the prayer belong together. When the Lord comes, he will judge, and he will gather his people.

The Bible's last book ends with the same prayer: “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20). The church has prayed it from the beginning.
passages.asks:
The earliest believers prayed ‘Our Lord, come’. Ask whether you pray for Christ's coming, or only for what you need now. And notice that Paul's last word is not the curse. It is ‘My love be with all of you’. Ask who needs to hear that from you.

1 Corinthians ends here. The story of Paul and this church goes on in 2 Corinthians, where their relationship is tested further.
